svg.text: RFC-100 blob cleaner, trimmed proposal: scenarios
arrow colors: blue = writer, grey = cleaner action, green = cleaner read, red = physical delete, orange = abort / refuse. Orange dashed band = inside the transaction lock.
1. Normal workflow: a blob reference is superseded, its file expires, the blob is deleted in the same clean
Row r in file group FG-A points at external blob P. The row is updated to point at Q. When F1 falls out of retention, P is the only thing that still mentions it. Watch for: nothing is
tombstoned by the clean; the registry entry (P, F1) dies later, in MDT compaction.

add F1
t1 COMPLETED
commit t2
write F2 (FG-A): row r -> Q
insert (Q, F2)
add F2
t2 COMPLETED

base/log file)
T0 = instant set of the cleaner's
DEDICATED MDT reader = {t1, t2}; no

C1 COMPLETED
Later, MDT compaction of blob_refs: the compaction filter drops (P, F1) because F1 is absent from FILES. Until then the stale entry is harmless: any lookup that finds it also finds F1 missing from
FILES and treats it as dead.
2. Concurrent writer re-references P while clean C1 is verifying it (C2 delete-and-re-add, R1)
Same setup: F1 (expired) references P. Writer W wants to commit F3 that also references P. There are exactly three places W's commit can land relative to C1's verification. Each is shown. In
none of them is P deleted while F3 references it.

P retained (deferred). It is re-derived when F3 itself expires.

Why there is no fourth case: the writer's commit path holds one lock across preCommit -> MDT write -> saveAsComplete, and Step B holds the same lock. So W is either fully before T0 (timing A), fully
inside (T0, Step B] (timing B), or after the plan is visible (timing C). Trade-off of plan-time verification: the veto window runs from REQUESTED to COMPLETED, so an async clean stuck in REQUESTED
blocks writers that re-reference P for that long. v2 only vetoed during the INFLIGHT drain.
3. Cross-file-group sharing and replace commits (C3, C7): the common case for external blobs
P is referenced from two file groups in two partitions. Then clustering replaces FG-A. Watch for: liveness uses raw FILES membership, not the file-system view, because the view hides
replaced file groups that are still readable by time travel.
Writer
Timeline + lock
Cleaner
blob_refs (MDT)
FILES (MDT)
Storage
P shared: F1 (FG-A, partition p1) and F5 (FG-B, partition p2). F1 expires in clean C1.
enumerate F1 -> {P}
prefix scan P -> {(P, F1), (P, F5)}
F5 present (partition p2) -> LIVE
P retained. One FILES lookup per distinct partition among the entries,
cached for the clean.
clustering: FG-A replaced by FG-C; the pointer to P is copied into F7. FG-A's files stay on disk inside retention.
replacecommit: write F7 (FG-C) with r -> P
insert (P, F7). Nothing happens to (P, F1): entries die only with their file.
later: row r updated in FG-C to Q, F7's old slice expires, P becomes a candidate again
prefix scan P -> {(P, F1), (P, F5), (P,
F1 still listed in FILES (replaced FG, within retention) -> LIVE
If the cleaner had asked the file-system view instead, getAllFileGroups would have filtered FG-A out as replaced, (P, F1) would look dead, and P would be deleted while a time-travel query inside the
retention window can still read FG-A. That is the C7 trap. Raw FILES membership avoids it.
when FG-A's replaced files and F5 finally expire, each of those cleans re-derives P from the expired file;
the last one finds no live entry and deletes P
4. MOR: a log update shadows the base file's reference (C4, R3), then compaction
FG-A has base F1 (row r -> P) and log L1 (row r -> Q). The base ref to P is dead logically but F1 physically still contains it. Watch for: P is over-retained until F1 dies, never
under-retained; log reads are fenced to completed instants.
Writer
Timeline + lock
Cleaner
blob_refs (MDT)
FILES (MDT)
Storage
steady state: slice {F1, L1} is the latest slice. Nothing expires, nothing is cleaned.
(P, F1) and (Q, L1) are both live
entries; the registry does not know that
L1 shadows F1 and does not need to
compaction writes base F2 (row r -> Q). Old slice {F1, L1} expires in clean C1.
enumerate F1 -> {P}; enumerate L1 through the instant-range-validated log reader -> {Q} (a block from a
failed, not-yet-rolled-back commit is never read)
scan P -> {(P, F1)}: only in C1's own
expired set -> survivor
scan Q -> {(Q, L1), (Q, F2)}
F2 present -> Q LIVE -> retained
delete F1, L1, and blob P
Rollback resurrection is safe for the same reason: if the log update in L1 had been rolled back before compaction, P would simply still be referenced by the retained F1, and (P, F1) never left the
registry. Over-retention is the only MOR degradation.
5. Rollback of a failed commit, and restore to a savepoint (C9)
A writer references P and dies before completing. Separately, the table is restored to an older savepoint. Watch for: the registry and FILES move together because they ride the same MDT
commit; the one unrecoverable case is spelled out.
Writer
Timeline + lock
Cleaner
blob_refs (MDT)
FILES (MDT)
Storage
rollback: writer W writes F3 (r -> P), MDT delta commit lands, W crashes before saveAsComplete
write F3 with r -> P
insert (P, F3) in W's MDT delta commit
crash: W never reaches COMPLETED
Step A while W is inflight: (P, F3) is
hidden by the completed-instant fence;
it is neither a retain vote nor a delete
vote
rollback of W: the whole MDT delta
commit is rolled back, so (P, F3) and
FILES' F3 disappear together
The liveness predicate never observes a half-state: either both the registry entry and the FILES entry are visible, or neither is. If W had completed instead of crashing, its blobRefsWritten flag
would have forced the cleaner to re-verify (timing B). Safety never rests on inflight entries. Rollback removes the whole MDT delta commit, so the hidden entries disappear with it. Separately, if F3
was the only file referencing managed P, rollback hands P to the next clean as a candidate (C9).
restore: table restored to savepoint S, which predates the commit that removed the last reference to P
restore to S
partition delete-and-rebuild via the async indexer (shouldDeletePartitionOnRestore = true for blob_refs)
partition is inflight -> verification
refuses to authorize any delete; every
candidate defers until the rebuild
completes
Unrecoverable case: a blob hard-deleted by a clean that completed before the restore, where the restored state references it. With same-clean deletion there is no window. This is exactly what the
optional grace window and queue buy; if a savepoint/restore SLA matters, enable them and size grace to that SLA. The file-slice cleaner has the same gap for data files today.
6. Failure handling: enumeration failure, crash mid-execution, plan replay, lock modes, table-internal paths
Five things that go wrong in practice. Each resolves to retain, retry, or refuse. None resolves to delete.
Writer
Timeline + lock
Cleaner
blob_refs (MDT)
FILES (MDT)
Storage
a) a file's blob column cannot be read at plan time
enumerate F1 -> FAILS (corrupt footer, unreadable block)
remove F1 from C1's delete set: keep the slice, warn, metric, retry
next cycle
v2 said proceed-and-flag. That deletes F1, never enqueues its paths, and the sweep only reclaims registry entries, so every blob referenced only by F1 is a permanent orphan (R2).
b) crash during execution
delete F1 ok; crash before blob P is deleted
C1 is INFLIGHT: re-execution re-reads
the plan sidecar and deletes P.
FileNotFound = success. No liveness
re-check is needed because the list was
verified under the lock and the veto has
protected it since.
c) plan replay
requestClean finds C0's completed file
empty: it replays C0's plan under a NEW
instant without re-planning
keep C0's plan sidecar list as-is; run it through the FULL verify
again (fresh T0, locked flag check) before deleting
C0's files are already deleted, so the list cannot be re-derived from them; stripping it would orphan every path only they referenced (R2). Re-verifying it catches the other direction: C0 already
deleted its blobs, the user re-creates P, a writer commits a reference to P, and a blind replay would delete the now-live P. Pending REQUESTED / INFLIGHT plans are a different case and run unchanged.
d) lock modes
Multi-writer with an external lock provider: supported. Single writer, all services inline: safe by sequentiality (clean runs in the writer's thread after endStateChange). Single writer + async

services + MDT: auto InProcessLockProvider, supported. Standalone HoodieCleaner process on a single-writer table: NO cross-process exclusion, and auto-adjust silently replaces a user-set provider with
InProcessLockProvider when all services are inline. Blob deletion must fail fast there.
e) table-internal paths
candidate path parses as a Hudi base or log file (e.g. a Lance DESCRIPTOR self-reference with managed =
true that leaked through a Parquet writer) -> never a candidate, never deleted
A blanket 'skip anything under the table base path' is wrong: RFC-100 Phase 3 puts Hudi-managed blobs under <base>/.hoodie/blobs/, which must stay eligible. Exclude by file-name shape
(FSUtils.isBaseFile / isLogFile) and reject such references at write time in every writer, not just the Lance one.
